stem: Where did the Texas cattle drives of 1866 head?

stimulus.source_note: Joseph G. McCoy, Historic Sketches of the Cattle Trade of the West and Southwest (1874), ch. 2. Public domain. Text verified against the 1874 edition as quoted in the Stanford-adjacent SVHS lesson (svhs.co/lesson/d1-5-9-12/) and the SweetStudy transcription of the same chapter.
stimulus.text:
Joseph G. McCoy, Historic Sketches of the Cattle Trade of the West and Southwest (1874), Chapter 2:

"Many ranchmen entirely neglected their stock, for they were regarded as not worth caring for. Stocks of cattle were, in certain sections, offered at prices ranging from one to two dollars per head, and that often without finding a purchaser. ... a select, matured animal, worth five or six dollars in Texas — was worth in the Northern markets more than ten times that amount."

"We have heard the number of cattle that had crossed Red river during 1866 put down as high as 260,000 head."

"Twenty-five to thirty-five days is the usual time required to bring a drove from Red river to the southern line of Kansas, a distance of between two hundred and fifty and three hundred miles..."

options.text: To the gold mines of California
options.misconception: Background: the drives went north to Kansas railheads, not west to California's mines.

options.text: To the buffalo ranges of Montana
options.misconception: Background: Montana's ranges came later, as ranching spread north; the 1866 drives aimed at Kansas.

options.text: To the ports of the Gulf Coast for shipment overseas
options.misconception: Background: the cattle went north overland to the railroads, not south to Gulf ports.

options.text: To Kansas railroad towns, to be shipped east for slaughter

rationales.A: Background: McCoy's droves walked north from the Red River to Kansas, not west to California.
rationales.B: Background: Montana ranching grew later. In 1866 the destination was the Kansas railhead, a 25- to 35-day drive.
rationales.C: Background: the herds moved north to the railroads. Gulf ports played no part in McCoy's account of the drives.
rationales.D: McCoy's geography is plain: 25 to 35 days from the Red River to the southern line of Kansas, where the herds met the railroad and the cars east.
rationales.general:
A drive needs a destination, and McCoy gives the road and the time.
1. Trace the route: north from the Red River, 250 to 300 miles, 25 to 35 days.
2. Find the end of the trail: the southern line of Kansas, where the railroad waited.
3. Name the purpose. Cattle walked to the rails so the rails could carry them east.
Remember: a trail always ends where a faster way of moving begins.
